The process converts nameplate motor power to full-load current, applies a 125% sizing multiplier, and selects the next larger standard breaker rating. The following formulas and worked example demonstrate the complete calculation procedure used by this motor protection calculator:

[web-kwcalc-com-motor-breaker-size-calculator-nec-motor-protecti.md] (dated 2026) In NEC Article 430, the 125% factor applies to branch-circuit conductors (430.22), and overload relays are set at 115% to 125% of nameplate current (430.32). The branch-circuit breaker is governed by NEC 430.52, which sets a maximum rather than a minimum: up to 250% of the table full-load current for an inverse-time breaker. Sizing the breaker at 125% of FLC, as this calculator does, is a conservative starting point; if it trips during motor starting, it may be increased up to the Table 430.52 limit.

 The most current version of the NEC is the 2026 edition . It superseded the 2023 edition, and the 2029 edition is expected to be released in late 2028. The 2026 edition of the NEC features modifications working toward proposed textual reorganizations  meant to modernize and enhance the usability of the code for the 2029 edition. Modernizing the existing document structure of the NEC will better reflect ever-evolving electrical infrastructure configurations and technological advancements and help support its users.

[web-nfpa-org-learn-more-about-nfpa-70-national-electrical-cod.md] (dated 2026) In some capacity, the NEC is utilized and enforced  in all 50 states in the U.S. It should be noted that, often based on the local legislative process, many states may enforce editions of the NEC that are not the most current. In some cases, municipalities within states will incorporate an edition of the NEC by reference into their locally amended  electrical code, such as in the case of Chicago and New York City. In these cases, it is possible that the local city authorities may be enforcing an entirely different edition of the NEC than the rest of the state; therefore, it is important to check with local jurisdictions as to which edition of the NEC is being enforced in the area.

[web-electricalflux-com-motor-breaker-size-chart-nec-article-430-sizing-.md] (dated 2026) Sizing a breaker for an AC motor is fundamentally different from sizing one for a resistive load like a baseboard heater. Motors are inductive and draw massive inrush current—known as Locked Rotor Amps (LRA)—during startup. If you size the breaker to the motor's normal running current, it will trip instantly every time you flip the switch. The direct answer: for a standard single-phase AC motor on an inverse-time thermal-magnetic breaker, multiply the motor's Full Load Amps (FLA) by 2.5 (250%) and round up to the next standard breaker size per NEC 240.6.

[web-electricalflux-com-motor-breaker-size-chart-nec-article-430-sizing-.md] (dated 2026) Start by identifying your system voltage (115V or 230V) and locating the corresponding Full Load Amps (FLA) column. The FLA represents the current the motor draws while running at its rated load and speed. The fourth column applies the NEC 430.52 rule, multiplying the 230V FLA by 2.5 to accommodate the startup inrush current without nuisance tripping. Finally, the fifth column maps that calculated value to the nearest standard breaker size available at your electrical supplier (e.g., 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70A). If the exact calculated value matches a standard size, use it; if it falls between sizes, you must round up.

[web-electricalflux-com-motor-breaker-size-chart-nec-article-430-sizing-.md] (dated 2026) Step 4: The Startup Exception. Install the breaker and test motor startup. If the high inrush current still trips the breaker instantly (common with high-inertia loads like large blowers or deep well pumps), invoke NEC 430.52(C)(1)(b). Step up to the next standard size (e.g., move from 35A to 40A). Final Result: 40A Breaker.

[web-electricalflux-com-motor-breaker-size-chart-nec-article-430-sizing-.md] (dated 2026) Three-Phase Motors: The chart above is strictly for single-phase AC motors. Three-phase motors draw significantly less current per horsepower. A 5 HP three-phase motor at 230V only draws about 15.2A, requiring a much smaller 40A breaker. Always consult NEC Table 430.250 for three-phase FLA values.

[web-kwcalc-com-motor-breaker-size-calculator-nec-motor-protecti.md] (dated 2026) Determine the correct circuit breaker size for single-phase and three-phase electric motors using NEC 125% motor protection rules, full-load current calculations, and standard breaker ratings.

Motors are inductive and draw massive inrush current—known as Locked Rotor Amps (LRA)—during startup. If you size the breaker to the motor's normal running current, it will trip instantly every time you flip the switch. The direct answer: for a standard single-phase AC motor on an inverse-time thermal-magnetic breaker, multiply the motor's Full Load Amps (FLA) by 2.5 (250%) and round up to the next standard breaker size per NEC 240.6.

[web-nfpa-org-learn-more-about-nfpa-70-national-electrical-cod.md] (dated 2026) Editions and Enforcement
 The most current version of the NEC is the 2026 edition . It superseded the 2023 edition, and the 2029 edition is expected to be released in late 2028. The 2026 edition of the NEC features modifications working toward proposed textual reorganizations  meant to modernize and enhance the usability of the code for the 2029 edition. Modernizing the existing document structure of the NEC will better reflect ever-evolving electrical infrastructure configurations and technological advancements and help support its users.

[web-nfpa-org-learn-more-about-nfpa-70-national-electrical-cod.md] (dated 2026) In some capacity, the NEC is utilized and enforced  in all 50 states in the U.S. It should be noted that, often based on the local legislative process, many states may enforce editions of the NEC that are not the most current. In some cases, municipalities within states will incorporate an edition of the NEC by reference into their locally amended  electrical code, such as in the case of Chicago and New York City. In these cases, it is possible that the local city authorities may be enforcing an entirely different edition of the NEC than the rest of the state; therefore, it is important to check with local jurisdictions as to which edition of the NEC is being enforced in the area.

[web-nfpa-org-learn-more-about-nfpa-70-national-electrical-cod.md] (dated 2026) While a lag in using the most current edition of the NEC is common, it may have a negative impact on electrical installations within communities. A study from the NFPA Fire & Life Safety Policy Institute  finds that not adhering to the latest edition of the NEC can lead to serious shortfalls in electrical safety for citizens and a failure to protect first responders and workers from preventable dangers.

[web-nfpa-org-learn-more-about-nfpa-70-national-electrical-cod.md] (dated 2026) Chapter 8, restructured in the 2026 edition of the NEC, now governs communication systems both outside and entering buildings. This chapter is no longer independent and is subject to the general provisions of Chapters 1 through 4.

[web-nfpa-org-learn-more-about-nfpa-70-national-electrical-cod.md] (dated 2026) What changed in the 2026 NEC?
 Similar to the changes made to the 2023 NEC, there were numerous structural changes made to the 2026 edition of the NEC. The technical committees moved articles around to make room for the more significant structural shift coming for the 2029 edition. Read more about the 2026 changes in this blog.

[web-nfpa-org-nfpa-70-nec-code-development.md] (dated 2026) Please note: The NEC® Correlating Committee and Code-Making Panels 1–18 are working on a comprehensive reorganization and restructuring of NFPA 70®, National Electrical Code® (NEC®) . This effort first began in the 2023 edition of the NEC, with the inclusion of new articles covering electrical installations over 1000 volts ac, 1500 volts dc, and with the relocation of content covering limited-energy systems in Chapter 7. More reorganization changes have occurred in the 2026 edition with the goal of completing the reorganization in the 2029 edition. More information on this ongoing initiative can be found at the link above. For information on the revision cycle for the 2029 edition of the NEC, please click the “Next Edition” tab below.
